pos: n. (the sharp weapon of an insect or serpent; that which wounds fatally)
etymology: Greek kentron, a sharp point — a goad, or the sting of a scorpion or bee. The same word appears in the goad against which it is hard to kick. Old English stingan, to pierce.
biblical_def: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? Paul is quoting Hosea and doing so in triumph, at the end of the longest sustained argument about resurrection in Scripture. The taunt only works because of what precedes it: the dead raised incorruptible, the corruptible having put on incorruption, death swallowed up in victory. And Paul does not leave the figure unexplained. The next verse takes the metaphor apart with a precision that is almost legal: the sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. Death is dangerous the way a scorpion is dangerous — because of its sting, and the sting is sin. Remove the sin and what is left is not a weakened enemy but a disarmed one. And sin's own power comes from the law, which pronounces the sentence that gives sin its lethal force; the wages of sin is death. So the chain runs backward: law gives sin its strength, sin gives death its sting, and death holds the race. Paul then names how the chain is broken, and it is not by human effort at any link: thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Christ bore the law's sentence, and the sting was spent in him. The believer still dies; he does not die stung.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a sharp-pointed weapon with which certain animals are furnished; anything that gives acute pain; the point or part that wounds.
webster_full: STING, n. A sharp-pointed weapon of some insects and other animals, with which they wound.
STING, n. Anything that gives acute pain, bodily or mental; as the stings of remorse.
STING, v.t. To pierce with the sharp-pointed instrument with which certain animals are furnished; to pain acutely.
GOAD, n. A pointed instrument used to stimulate a beast to move faster.
VICTORY, n. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest.
scriptures: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
corruption_summary: Death is domesticated as a natural stage of life or denied as an enemy at all; Paul treats it as a real foe with a real weapon, disarmed only because Christ absorbed the sentence that armed it.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern funeral has largely adopted the view that death is natural — a return, a passage, part of the order of things — and the language of enemy and victory sounds overwrought against it. Scripture calls death the last enemy that shall be destroyed, and traces it not to creation but to the fall: by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin. This is why the Lord wept at the grave of a man he was about to raise. Death is an intruder, and a Christianity that has learned to call it a friend has stopped needing a resurrection. Paul's taunt is not bravado about a natural process; it is the mockery of a defeated enemy.

The opposite loss occurs where the verse is quoted without the one that follows it. O death, where is thy sting is read at funerals constantly, and the sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law rarely is. But the taunt is only warranted for those for whom the sting has actually been drawn. Christ did not abolish death by declaring it harmless; he bore the law's sentence against sin in his own body, and the sting was spent there. Cut the explanation and the triumph becomes a sentiment addressed to everyone, which empties it. Kept whole, it is the strongest comfort in Scripture and it is addressed to those who are in Christ Jesus.
roots_summary: Greek kentron (G2759), a sharp point, a sting or goad; nikos (G3534), victory; hades (G86), the grave; hamartia (G266), sin.
roots_lines: Greek kentron (G2759) — a sting, a goad; rendered sting, and pricks in the Damascus road account.
Greek nikos (G3534) — victory; used three times in this closing passage.
Greek hades (G86) — the unseen realm, the grave; rendered grave in the taunt.
Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, a missing of the mark; identified as the sting itself.
Greek katapino (G2666) — to swallow up; death is swallowed up in victory.
usage: “O death, where is thy sting?” — a taunt over a disarmed enemy.
“the sting of death is sin” — the metaphor explained.
“the strength of sin is the law” — the chain traced to its first link.

etymology: Hebrew zera, seed or sowing, from zara, to scatter seed. The Authorized Version compounds it with time to render the season of sowing, first of the six pairs in God's promise after the flood.
biblical_def: While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease. The promise is given after the flood, and its form is worth noticing: six pairs, each a rhythm rather than a state. Seedtime with harvest, cold with heat, summer with winter, day with night. God does not promise uninterrupted mildness; he promises that the alternation will hold. The cold is guaranteed along with the heat, and the night along with the day. This is the foundation of what theologians call common grace — the ordinary reliability of the created order, extended to everyone without distinction. The Lord states the principle in his own words: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. Paul preached the same to pagans at Lystra, saying that God left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness. Two things follow. All settled agriculture, science, and ordinary planning rest on a promise God made to Noah, whether or not the planners know it. And the promise has a stated limit: while the earth remaineth. The seasons are guaranteed until the end, not for ever, and Peter builds a warning on exactly that reservation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the season proper for sowing; the season of sowing seed.
webster_full: SEED-TIME, n. The season proper for sowing.
SEED, n. The substance, animal or vegetable, which nature prepares for the reproduction and conservation of the species.
HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected.
SEASON, n. One of the four divisions of the year, spring, summer, autumn, winter; a fit or suitable time.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons; in theology, God's promise and engagement.
scriptures: While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.
And I will establish my covenant with you; neither shall all flesh be cut off any more by the waters of a flood; neither shall there any more be a flood to destroy the earth.
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.
corruption_summary: The regularity of nature is taken as a self-explaining property of a closed system; Scripture presents it as a covenant promise, freely given, and expressly bounded by the end of the age.
corruption_paragraphs: The uniformity of nature is the working assumption of every science and of all ordinary life, and it is generally treated as a brute fact needing no explanation — things have always gone on this way, therefore they will. Genesis 8:22 gives the ground of it, and the ground is personal: God said this would hold. That does not make the study of nature suspect; it makes it possible, and the Christian doctrine of creation is a large part of why the natural sciences arose where they did. What it denies is that the regularity is self-sustaining. The seasons are kept by a promise, not by the universe's own resources.

Peter takes up this exact point and turns it into a warning. He describes scoffers who say, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation — an argument from uniformity against the return of Christ. His answer is that they willingly forget the flood, the one occasion when the ordinary course did not continue, and the reservation written into the promise itself: while the earth remaineth. The rhythms are guaranteed until the end and not past it. A man who builds on the permanence of seedtime and harvest has read half the sentence.
roots_summary: Hebrew zera (H2233), seed, sowing; qatsir (H7105), harvest; qor (H7120), cold; berith (H1285), covenant.
roots_lines: Hebrew zera (H2233) — seed, sowing; the first term of the first pair.
Hebrew qatsir (H7105) — harvest, the reaping season; paired with seedtime.
Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, to rest; shall not cease.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; established with Noah and every living creature.
Hebrew owd (H5750) — again, any more; neither shall there any more be a flood.
usage: “seedtime and harvest” — the first of six guaranteed rhythms.
“cold and heat” — the hard half promised with the pleasant.
“while the earth remaineth” — the limit written into the promise.

pos: n. (the vital juice of a plant; that which sustains growth)
etymology: Hebrew saba, to be satisfied or filled to the full — the Authorized Version's full of sap renders a single word meaning well-watered, satisfied. Old English sæp, the juice of a plant.
biblical_def: The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted. The psalm is a long catalogue of God's works in creation, and this line is doing something specific with the cedars. They are the largest, most valuable, most sought-after timber in the ancient Near East — the trees kings imported for palaces and temples. The psalmist calls them the trees of the LORD, and adds the decisive clause: which he hath planted. Nobody planted the cedars of Lebanon. They grew where no man sowed, on mountains no man terraced, and they were full of sap — thriving, well-watered, alive — entirely apart from human cultivation. The surrounding verses keep the same emphasis: he causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man. God is portrayed as the actual gardener of the world, and the psalm shows him feeding beasts and birds that no one farms. The image of inward sap as the mark of real life carries through Scripture in the places one would expect. The blessed man of Psalm 1 shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither. Jeremiah says such a man shall not be careful in the year of drought. And the Lord names the source directly: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the juice of plants of any kind, which flows chiefly between the wood and the bark; the vital juice.
webster_full: SAP, n. The juice of plants of any kind, which flows chiefly between the wood and the bark.
SAPPY, a. Abounding with sap; juicy; succulent; young; not firm; weak.
CEDAR, n. The name of different species of trees; the cedar of Lebanon is a large and durable tree, much valued for building.
HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labors in tillage.
FLOURISH, v.i. To thrive; to grow luxuriantly; to increase and enlarge, as a healthy growing plant.
scriptures: The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted;
He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth;
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
corruption_summary: Creation is treated either as raw material with no relation to God or as itself divine; Psalm 104 presents a world God actively tends, distinct from him and belonging to him.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors are live at once. The materialist account treats the natural world as resource — valuable in proportion to its use, with no owner above the user. The pantheist and neo-pagan account, which has been gaining ground for a generation, treats nature as itself sacred, and slides easily into the worship of the creature more than the Creator. Psalm 104 grants what is true in the second and denies its conclusion. The cedars are magnificent and full of life, and they are the trees of the LORD, planted by him. They are neither commodity nor deity; they are his property, and that is the ground of both their dignity and their limits.

The practical corollary is a doctrine of stewardship that owes nothing to either camp. A Christian cares for creation because it belongs to God and man was placed in the garden to dress it and to keep it, not because the earth is sacred and not merely because resources are scarce. And the figure has an inward application the Bible presses hardest. Sap is invisible; a tree full of it and a tree dying look similar from a distance and are distinguished by fruit in season and a leaf that does not wither. That is exactly the test Psalm 1 applies to a man, and the Lord applies to a branch: abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
roots_summary: Hebrew saba (H7646), to be satisfied or filled; ets (H6086), a tree; erez (H730), a cedar; nata (H5193), to plant.
roots_lines: Hebrew saba (H7646) — to be satisfied, filled to the full; rendered full of sap.
Hebrew ets (H6086) — a tree, wood; the trees of the LORD.
Hebrew erez (H730) — a cedar; the great timber of Lebanon.
Hebrew nata (H5193) — to plant, to fix; the decisive clause, which he hath planted.
Greek georgos (G1092) — a husbandman, a tiller; the Father in John 15:1.
usage: “the trees of the LORD are full of sap” — life no man cultivated.
“which he hath planted” — the clause that assigns ownership.
“his leaf also shall not wither” — the same figure, of a man.

pos: n. (the implement that breaks ground for sowing)
etymology: Greek arotron, a plough, from aroo, to till. Old English ploh. The Authorized Version keeps the older spelling; the American plow is the same word. The ancient plough was guided one-handed while the other hand drove the team, which is why looking back ruins the furrow.
biblical_def: And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God. The saying answers a man who had offered to follow the Lord but asked first to go bid farewell to those at his house — a request that sounds entirely reasonable and is refused. The force of the image depends on the tool. An ancient plough was light, guided with one hand while the other managed the oxen, and it cut a shallow furrow that had to be kept straight by the ploughman's eye fixed on a point ahead. A man who turns his head wanders, and a wandering furrow ruins the row. The Lord is not condemning affection for family; he is describing the divided attention that makes a man unfit for the work. The word fit is a word of usefulness, not of worthiness — such a man is not disqualified from grace but unserviceable for the task. Elijah's call of Elisha stands behind the exchange and sharpens it. Elisha was ploughing when the mantle was cast on him, asked leave to kiss his father and mother, and was granted it — then slew his oxen and burned the plough and followed. The prophet burned the equipment so there was nothing to go back to. And the Lord adds the shortest warning in Scripture to the same point: Remember Lot's wife.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an instrument for turning up, breaking and preparing the ground for receiving the seed.
webster_full: PLOUGH, PLOW, n. An instrument for turning up, breaking and preparing the ground for receiving the seed.
PLOUGH, v.t. To turn up, break and prepare for seed with a plough; to furrow.
PLOUGHMAN, n. One who ploughs or holds a plough; a cultivator of the earth.
FURROW, n. A trench in the earth made by a plough.
FIT, a. Suitable; convenient; meet; becoming; qualified; competent for the purpose.
scriptures: And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
So he departed thence, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.

And he left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, Let me, I pray thee, kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow thee. And he said unto him, Go back again: for what have I done to thee?
corruption_summary: Discipleship is presented as an addition to an otherwise unchanged life, with commitment kept revocable; the Lord names an undivided attention and treats the backward look as disqualifying for the work.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant presentation of Christianity in the West asks for a decision and then leaves the life largely as it was, with faith added as one commitment among others and the option of stepping back always open. Luke 9 is a series of three encounters designed to dismantle that arrangement, and each candidate is turned away or warned over something reasonable — a place to sleep, a father's funeral, a farewell. The Lord is not being harsh about family duties, which he elsewhere enforces against those who evaded them by religious pretext. He is refusing a following that keeps one eye behind it, because such a following cannot do the work.

The opposite distortion turns the saying into a threat against every believer who looks back with longing, and there is a real pastoral cost to that misuse. The word is fit — useful, serviceable — and the subject is fitness for labour in the kingdom, not the security of a soul. Peter looked back thoroughly enough to deny his Lord three times and was restored and commissioned. The saying is a call to undivided attention, not a verdict on the faltering. Elisha's example shows the positive form: he was permitted his farewell, and then he burned the plough, which is the difference between a man who has said goodbye and a man who has kept the option.
roots_summary: Greek arotron (G723), a plough; euthetos (G2111), well-placed, fit for use; opiso (G3694), behind, backward; Hebrew charash (H2790), to plough.
roots_lines: Greek arotron (G723) — a plough; its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek euthetos (G2111) — well-placed, useful, fit; a word of serviceability, not of worth.
Greek opiso (G3694) — behind, back; looking back.
Hebrew charash (H2790) — to plough, to engrave; what Elisha was doing when called.
Hebrew addereth (H155) — a mantle, a glorious cloak; cast on Elisha at the plough.
usage: “having put his hand to the plough” — a one-handed tool needing a fixed eye.
“is fit for the kingdom of God” — serviceable, not worthy.
“Remember Lot's wife” — the shortest warning to the same point.

pos: n. (a standard or staff on which something is lifted up)
etymology: Hebrew nes, a standard, a banner, an ensign lifted up to be seen from far off — the same word rendered banner and ensign elsewhere. The Authorized Version's pole understates it; what Moses raised was a signal-standard.
biblical_def: And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live. The remedy is deliberately strange. Israel is dying of serpent bites, and God's provision is an image of the very thing killing them, lifted up where all can see, healing by nothing but a look. No medicine is applied and no work is required; the verb is looketh. Moses obeyed, and the result is recorded exactly: if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived. The Hebrew nes means a standard raised as a rallying signal, which is why the object could save a whole camp at once — it was visible from anywhere. The Lord himself supplies the interpretation, and it is the only place in the Gospels where he explains an Old Testament type of his own death: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. The likeness is precise at every point. The thing lifted bears the form of the curse; it is raised publicly; and life comes by looking, which is to say by faith and not by contribution. The sequel is equally instructive: the brazen serpent was kept, and centuries later Israel was burning incense to it, until Hezekiah broke it in pieces and called it Nehushtan, a piece of brass.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a long slender piece of wood, or the stem of a small tree deprived of its branches; a staff.
webster_full: POLE, n. A long slender piece of wood, or the stem of a small tree deprived of its branches.
POLE, n. A staff; a long stick; a pole on which a standard or ensign is raised.
ENSIGN, n. The flag or banner of a military band; a signal; a badge; a standard.
BANNER, n. A square flag; a standard; a streamer borne at the end of a lance or elsewhere.
BRAZEN, a. Pertaining to brass; made of brass; as a brazen helmet.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.
And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up:

He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.
corruption_summary: The episode is treated as folklore or reduced to a moral about obedience; the Lord makes it a type of his own crucifixion, and the sequel supplies Scripture's own warning about venerating a genuine relic.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments assign Numbers 21 to folk etiology — a story invented later to explain a bronze cult object kept in the temple. The Lord's own use of the passage forecloses that reading for anyone who takes his words as authoritative. He treats the event as history and as a divinely intended pattern of his death, using the strongest language of necessity: even so must the Son of man be lifted up. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the historicity of the wilderness narratives, and notes that this particular type is not an interpreter's ingenuity but the Lord's own exposition.

The moralising reduction is more common in preaching: the serpent as a lesson about obedience or about facing one's troubles. That empties the one feature the passage insists on. The dying Israelite contributes nothing but a look; the healing is entirely in the object God provided. That is justification by faith in narrative form, and Paul's doctrine is in seed here. The sequel is the second warning and it is severe. The brazen serpent was real, God-commanded, and genuinely used to save lives — and it became an idol receiving incense, until a reforming king smashed it and named it a piece of brass. A true relic of a true miracle is exactly the sort of thing that ends up worshipped, which is why Hezekiah's hammer is in the canon.
roots_summary: Hebrew nes (H5251), a standard or ensign; nachash (H5175), a serpent; saraph (H8314), fiery, a fiery serpent; nabat (H5027), to look intently.
roots_lines: Hebrew nes (H5251) — a signal-standard, an ensign; rendered pole, and banner elsewhere.
Hebrew saraph (H8314) — burning, a fiery serpent; the creature and the image alike.
Hebrew nachash (H5175) — a serpent; and nechosheth, brass, the pun behind Nehushtan.
Hebrew nabat (H5027) — to look, to regard attentively; the one thing required of the dying.
Greek hupsoo (G5312) — to lift up, to exalt; the Lord's word for his own crucifixion.
usage: “set it upon a pole” — a standard raised to be seen by all.
“when he looketh upon it, shall live” — healing by a look alone.
“he called it Nehushtan” — a true relic broken as an idol.

pos: n. (a swift long-eared animal, named among the unclean)
etymology: Hebrew arnebeth, the hare. Old English hara. The animal appears only in the two lists of creatures forbidden as food, where it is named with the camel and the coney as chewing the cud but not dividing the hoof.
biblical_def: And the hare, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you. The clean-animal law works by a two-part test, and the hare fails on the second half. An animal fit for Israel's table had to both chew the cud and part the hoof; the camel, the coney, and the hare met the first requirement and not the second, while the swine met the second and not the first. Meeting half the standard did not help. The description of the hare as chewing the cud has been a favourite target of critics, since the animal is not a ruminant in the modern zoological sense; but Moses is not writing a treatise on digestion. He is classifying animals by observable behaviour for a people who would identify them by sight, and the hare's constant grinding motion of the jaw is exactly what the phrase describes. The purpose of the whole system is stated at the end of the chapter and it is not hygiene: I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The dietary law was a daily, tangible instruction in separation — Israel could not eat a meal without being reminded that it belonged to God. And the same law is expressly set aside in the New Testament, when the Lord declared all meats clean and Peter was told on the housetop, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a quadruped of the genus Lepus, with long ears, a short tail, soft hair, and a divided upper lip; a timid animal, remarkable for its speed.
webster_full: HARE, n. A quadruped of the genus Lepus, with long ears, a short tail, soft hair, and a divided upper lip.
HARE, n. It is a timid animal, moves with remarkable swiftness, and is much hunted.
CONEY, n. A rabbit; in Scripture, a small animal that inhabits the rocks.
UNCLEAN, a. In the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; not cleansed by ritual observances; forbidden as food.
RUMINATE, v.i. To chew the cud; to chew again what has been slightly chewed and swallowed.
scriptures: And the hare, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you.
And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you.

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
corruption_summary: The dietary law is pressed into service as ancient public health or cited as proof of biblical error about animal biology; Scripture states its own purpose, which is holiness, and expressly ends the ordinance in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The hygienic explanation — that these laws were advanced ancient medicine, protecting Israel from trichinosis and the rest — is popular and is not what the text says. Leviticus 11 gives its own reason twice, and it is holiness: ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The hare carries no particular disease, and the shellfish and the rock badger are not a public health programme. The law was a system of separation, taught through the most repeated act of daily life, marking Israel off from the nations at every meal. Reading it as sanitation makes the law look clever and makes the New Testament's abolition of it look like a step backward.

The critical objection about the cud is worth answering plainly because it is raised so often. Moses writes as an observer addressing observers, using ordinary descriptive language about a jaw in constant motion, in a text meant to be applied in a field rather than a laboratory. Scripture speaks phenomenally throughout — of sunrise, of the four corners of the earth — without error, because it says what appears and means what it says. The doctrine of inerrancy concerns what the text affirms, and Leviticus 11 affirms which animals Israel may eat, not a taxonomy of digestion. And the ordinance itself is finished: the Lord declared all meats clean, and Peter was corrected for keeping a distinction God had removed.
roots_summary: Hebrew arnebeth (H768), the hare; gerah (H1625), the cud; parsah (H6541), a hoof; tame (H2931), unclean.
roots_lines: Hebrew arnebeth (H768) — the hare; named only in the two dietary lists.
Hebrew gerah (H1625) — the cud; the first half of the two-part test.
Hebrew parsah (H6541) — a hoof; the second half, which the hare fails.
Hebrew tame (H2931) — unclean, ceremonially defiled; the verdict on the animal.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to be set apart, to sanctify; the law's stated purpose.
usage: “he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof” — half the test is no help.
“ye shall be holy; for I am holy” — the law's own stated reason.
“what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” — the ordinance ended.

pos: n. (a wild ruminant; in the AV, the fallow deer)
etymology: Hebrew yachmur, the fallow deer or roebuck, from a root meaning red or ruddy. Old English deor, which once meant any wild animal and narrowed over time to this family. It appears in the list of clean wild game Israel might eat.
biblical_def: The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois. The list is the positive side of the dietary law, and its presence is easy to overlook. Having forbidden the hare, the camel, the coney, and the swine, Moses names seven wild animals Israel was free to hunt and eat. The law was not a regime of scarcity; it drew a line and left a great deal of ground inside it. These are all wild game, taken by hunting rather than raised, which also means the ordinary Israelite had access to meat beyond his flocks. The deer family runs through Scripture in the language of longing and of sure-footedness. The most famous instance is the psalm that gave the church one of its enduring pictures of spiritual thirst: as the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. Habakkuk uses the same animal for stability in hard country — he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. And Isaiah promises that in the restoration the lame man shall leap as an hart. A creature known for thirst, for speed, and for footing on broken ground turns out to be a natural figure for the life of faith, and Scripture uses it for all three.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a quadruped of the genus Cervus, of several species, as the stag or red deer, the fallow deer, and the roebuck.
webster_full: DEER, n. A quadruped of the genus Cervus, of several species, as the stag or red deer, the fallow deer, and the roebuck.
DEER, n. These animals are wild, and hunted in the chase; they are remarkable for fleetness.
HART, n. A stag or male deer, an animal of the cervine genus.
ROEBUCK, n. A species of deer, the smallest of the cervine genus, with erect cylindrical branched horns.
CHAMOIS, n. A species of goat, whose skin is made into soft leather.
scriptures: The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois.

Nevertheless these ye shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the cloven hoof; as the camel, and the hare, and the coney: for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you.
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.
corruption_summary: The law is remembered only for its prohibitions, and the goodness of creaturely provision within it is forgotten; Deuteronomy names what Israel could freely eat before naming what it could not.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the shape of the law itself. Deuteronomy 14 begins with a list of what may be eaten and then gives the exclusions, and the order is not accidental; the same pattern governs Eden, where every tree was given and one was withheld. A religion remembered chiefly by its prohibitions has been remembered badly. Paul writes against exactly that distortion when he names as a doctrine of devils the commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving, and adds that every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving.

The second matter is the use Scripture makes of this animal, which repays attention in a culture that treats spiritual desire as either sentiment or technique. The hart panting after water brooks is an image of thirst under duress — the psalm is written by a man whose tears have been his meat day and night and who is being asked, Where is thy God? Longing for God in the Bible is most often depicted in drought rather than in plenty. Habakkuk's hinds' feet come at the end of a book about invasion, and Isaiah's leaping hart belongs to a promise made to a lame man in a desert. The figure consistently belongs to people in hard country.
roots_summary: Hebrew yachmur (H3180), the fallow deer; ayyal (H354), a hart or stag; tsebi (H6643), a roebuck or gazelle; ayyalah (H355), a hind.
roots_lines: Hebrew yachmur (H3180) — the fallow deer; named among the clean wild game.
Hebrew ayyal (H354) — a hart, a stag; the animal of Psalm 42 and Isaiah 35.
Hebrew tsebi (H6643) — a roebuck, a gazelle; also the word for beauty or glory.
Hebrew ayyalah (H355) — a hind; hinds' feet in Habakkuk and Psalm 18.
Hebrew arag (H6165) — to long for, to pant; as the hart panteth.
usage: “the hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer” — what Israel could freely eat.
“as the hart panteth after the water brooks” — thirst under duress.
“Then shall the lame man leap as an hart” — the promise of restoration.

pos: n. (an aromatic reed used in the holy oil and incense)
etymology: Hebrew qaneh, a reed or stalk — the root behind the English cane and canon (a measuring reed). Sweet cane is the aromatic species imported for the sanctuary, named among the ingredients of the holy anointing oil.
biblical_def: Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money, neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities. Sweet cane was an imported aromatic, expensive, and required for the holy oil of the sanctuary; to withhold it was to economise on the worship of God. But the verse turns in a way the reader does not expect. God does not complain of being underfed. Two verses earlier he has said, I have not caused thee to serve with an offering, nor wearied thee with incense — the ceremonial burden was never onerous to Israel. The reversal is the point: thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities. The servant in the relationship turns out to be God, bearing what his people have loaded on him. And then, immediately, comes one of the great gospel sentences of the Old Testament: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins. Jeremiah preaches the same doctrine from the other side, where the cane is brought and is still refused: to what purpose cometh there to me incense from Sheba, and the sweet cane from a far country? your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices sweet unto me. Withheld offerings and lavish offerings meet the same verdict when the heart is wrong.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a reed; the stem of a small palm or reed; sweet cane, an aromatic reed used in the sacred oil and perfume.
webster_full: CANE, n. In botany, this term is applied to several species of plants belonging to different genera, such as arundo, calamus, saccharum.
CANE, n. A reed; the stem of a reed or small palm, used for a walking stick.
SWEET CANE, n. An aromatic reed or calamus, an ingredient of the holy anointing oil of the Hebrews.
CALAMUS, n. The sweet-scented flag or reed, the aromatic reed of the Scriptures.
INCENSE, n. Perfume exhaled by fire; the odors of spices and gums, burned in religious rites.
scriptures: Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money, neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
To what purpose cometh there to me incense from Sheba, and the sweet cane from a far country? your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices sweet unto me.
Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:
corruption_summary: Worship is treated as a transaction in which God is supplied and satisfied; Isaiah reverses the roles entirely, and grounds forgiveness in God's own name rather than in anything brought.
corruption_paragraphs: The transactional instinct in religion is universal and survives every reformation. It appears wherever attendance, giving, or service is felt to place God under some obligation, and the prosperity teaching is only its most explicit form. Isaiah 43 dismantles it from an unexpected angle. God says the ceremonial system never burdened Israel and that he has not been fed by it; what he has borne is their sin. The relationship runs the opposite way from the one the worshipper assumes. He is not the supplier and God the recipient; God is the one carrying the weight, and the sanctuary system was a gift to Israel rather than a service to God.

The ground of forgiveness in the next verse settles the matter beyond dispute. I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions — and the reason given is for mine own sake. Not for anything brought, not in response to reform, not because the sweet cane was finally purchased. Jeremiah shows the same God refusing offerings that were brought, at great expense, from a far country. Nothing in the hand changes the verdict; the pardon is free and is grounded in God's regard for his own name. That is why the Reformed tradition insists that even faith is not a contribution but an instrument, and why the sola in grace alone is doing real work.
roots_summary: Hebrew qaneh (H7070), a reed, sweet cane; machah (H4229), to blot out; abad (H5647), to serve; yaga (H3021), to weary.
roots_lines: Hebrew qaneh (H7070) — a reed, a measuring cane; sweet cane, an ingredient of the holy oil.
Hebrew abad (H5647) — to serve, to labour; God says Israel made him serve with their sins.
Hebrew yaga (H3021) — to toil, to weary; what their iniquities did to him.
Hebrew machah (H4229) — to wipe out, to blot; of transgressions, at verse 25.
Hebrew chelbah (H2459) — fat; the fat of thy sacrifices, the choicest portion.
usage: “thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money” — economising on worship.
“thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities” — the roles reversed.
“I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake” — the ground of pardon.

pos: n. (a round body; a thing easily thrown)
etymology: Hebrew dur, a circle or ball, from a root meaning to go round. The word occurs once, in a prophecy against a court official, and the image is of something small enough to be hurled a great distance without effort.
biblical_def: He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die, and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house. The prophecy is against Shebna, the treasurer over the royal household, and it is unusually personal. Isaiah has just found him cutting himself an impressive tomb in the rock — a man arranging his own monument — and God's answer is that he will be picked up and thrown out of the country like a ball. The comparison is chosen for its ease. Whatever Shebna's standing, he is a small round object in the hand that is about to throw him. And the detail about the chariots lands on exactly the thing he was proudest of: the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house. What he had accumulated as evidence of his importance becomes the record of his disgrace. Isaiah then names his replacement, and the contrast is the point of the whole passage: Eliakim is given the government, called a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and receives the key of the house of David laid upon his shoulder — so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. That sentence is taken up by the risen Christ in Revelation and applied to himself. A steward who built himself a tomb is thrown away; a steward who serves is given a key that the true Son of David finally claims.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a round body; a spherical substance, whether natural or artificial; anything round or spherical.
webster_full: BALL, n. A round body; a spherical substance, whether natural or artificial; or a body nearly round.
BALL, n. A bullet; a ball of iron or lead for cannon or small arms.
TOSS, v.t. To throw with the hand, especially to throw with the palm of the hand upward; to pitch; to fling.
STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and keep the accounts.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; a place in which the body of a deceased person is laid.
scriptures: He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die, and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house.
Behold, the LORD will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee.
And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.
The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
corruption_summary: Position and legacy are pursued as things a man secures for himself; Isaiah shows a senior official arranging his own monument and being thrown out of the country like a ball.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that office is stewardship and never property. Shebna was over the house — a real and important charge — and he treated it as a platform for his own standing, spending his energies on a rock-cut tomb and a stable of chariots. The rebuke is not that he held high office but that he used it to build a monument. Scripture's standard for every steward is the one Paul states: it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful. What a man does with an office he did not give himself is the whole test, and a great deal of what passes for legacy-building in church and public life would not survive it.

The turn at the end of the chapter is what makes the passage more than a warning. Eliakim replaces Shebna and is described in terms no bureaucrat could fill — a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, clothed with the robe, girded with the girdle, carrying the key of the house of David on his shoulder, opening and shutting with no appeal. The office outgrows the man immediately; Isaiah says a few verses later that even Eliakim, loaded with the whole glory of his father's house, will finally give way. The words find their rest only in the one who says of himself, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth. Every human steward is measured against a Steward who does not fail.
roots_summary: Hebrew dur (H1754), a ball or circle; tul (H2904), to hurl or cast; kabod (H3519), glory; maphteach (H4668), a key.
roots_lines: Hebrew dur (H1754) — a circle, a ball; rendered ball, its only such use.
Hebrew tul (H2904) — to cast, to hurl violently; rendered toss.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight; the chariots of thy glory.
Hebrew maphteach (H4668) — a key; laid on Eliakim's shoulder at verse 22.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house, household; Shebna was the man over it.
usage: “toss thee like a ball into a large country” — thrown without effort.
“the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame” — the pride turned to record.
“the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder” — the office that outgrows the man.

pos: n. (a crease or fold; a mark of age or wear)
etymology: Greek rhutis, a wrinkle or fold in cloth or skin. Old English wrinclian, to wind about. Paul pairs it with spot to describe what the church will not have when Christ presents her to himself.
biblical_def: That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. The verse states the purpose of Christ's love for the church, and the whole sentence is about what he does. He loved the church and gave himself for it; he sanctifies and cleanses it; he presents it to himself. The bride contributes nothing to her own adorning. Spot and wrinkle are drawn from cloth and from skin, and the pair covers both kinds of fault — the stain that comes from outside and the crease that comes from age and use. Neither will be found. The word present is a wedding word, and glorious here means splendid, arrayed; the picture is of a bride brought forward in full beauty, and the beauty is the bridegroom's gift. This is the church as she will be, not as she is, and the difference is the whole doctrine of sanctification running toward glorification. Paul is not describing a congregation any reader would recognise; he is describing what Christ is making. The passage is set inside instruction to husbands, and the logic runs from the greater to the lesser: husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it. A husband's self-giving is patterned on a love that takes full responsibility for what the beloved becomes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a small ridge or prominence, or a furrow, formed by the shrinking or contraction of any smooth substance; a crease in the skin or in cloth.
webster_full: WRINKLE, n. A small ridge or prominence, or a furrow, formed by the shrinking or contraction of any smooth substance.
WRINKLE, n. A crease or fold in the face or skin, usually the effect of age.
WRINKLE, v.t. To contract into furrows and prominences; to crease.
BLEMISH, n. Any mark of deformity; any scar or defect that diminishes beauty or renders imperfect.
PRESENT, v.t. To set, place or introduce into the presence of a superior; to exhibit to view.
scriptures: That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
corruption_summary: The verse is used either to demand a perfectionism no congregation can produce or to justify indifference about the church's actual condition; Paul describes a work Christ is doing and will finish.
corruption_paragraphs: Perfectionist and separatist movements read Ephesians 5:27 as a present standard and then go looking for the spotless church, which does not exist; the search produces either endless division as each new body proves flawed, or the pretence that one's own assembly has arrived. The tense of the passage forbids it. Christ might present the church so — a purpose still being worked out, whose completion belongs to the day of glorification. The Reformed tradition has always held that the visible church in this world is mixed and imperfect, and Paul wrote these words to a congregation he had to correct at length.

The opposite error takes the promise as a reason for complacency: since Christ will present her spotless, her present condition matters little. But the same sentence names the means — he sanctifies and cleanses her now — and the New Testament everywhere presses the church toward what she is becoming. Peter draws exactly this inference: seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless. The certainty of the end is the motive for effort, not a substitute for it. And the image guards a doctrine about Christ as well as about the church, since a bridegroom who takes responsibility for his bride's beauty is the pattern Paul then hands to every husband.

Greek spilos (G4696) — a spot, a stain; the fault that comes from outside.
Greek paristemi (G3936) — to present, to set beside; a word used of presenting a bride.
Greek amomos (G299) — unblemished, faultless; used of the sacrificial lamb and of the church.
Greek endoxos (G1741) — glorious, splendid; the church as she will be presented.
usage: “not having spot, or wrinkle” — stain from without, crease from within.
“that he might present it to himself” — the bridegroom does the adorning.
“be diligent that ye may be found of him… without spot” — the inference Peter draws.
